catalog_quote: 2.14. Stress. The stress is expiratory and strong. It is predictable; consequently, nonphonemic. Words containing no geminate vowel phonemes or diphthongs have the stress on the initial syllable. /axə/ [a´xxə̆] 'elder brother' /uŋšisəŋ/ [u̜´ŋšĭsă~] 'having read'. Words containing one geminate vowel phoneme or one diphthong have the stress on the geminate vowel or diphthong, respectively. /galuu/ [Gałū´] 'goose' /dalae/ [Dałae´] 'sea'. Words containing more than one geminate vowel phoneme or diphthong have the stress on the penultimate geminate vowel or diphthong. /moriooroo/ [mor⁽ⁱ⁾ō´rō] 'by means of his own horse' /dalaegaaraa/ [Dałăeγā´rā] 'by means of his own sea'. sweep_summary: Only one sweep item for halh1238: Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Books 3) = Hagberg 1993 University of Arizona dissertation 'An autosegmental theory of stress'. The Glottolog handle (MPG pure) and sil.org were bot-blocked (403), but an open scan of the 1993 dissertation is on archive.org (item an-autosegmental-theory-of-stress, third-party upload 2025); PDF (365 pp., text layer) and scanned text with and updated. Khalkha occupies pp. 192-195: rule 'first long vowel stressed, else first vowel', data from Street 1963, analysed as Weight-to-Stress (left-to-right, non-iterative) + End Rule Left. This is secondary (Street's data) and confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding; it refines the deciding Poppe 1970 quote only for words with 3+ long vowels (leftmost vs. penultimate long vowel), where Walker 1997's 'rightmost nonfinal heavy' also differs. It does not supersede Poppe/Walker. Also re-read the first-hand acoustic papers already on file from the 9/16 audit: Svantesson 1990 (intensity: first long vowel else initial; concludes no unified word stress), Sang & Martin 2012 (F0 highest on the long vowel, else initial; stress position predictable), Karlsson & Svantesson 2004 (reject lexical stress, prominence phrasal). Nothing left unacquired for this item; priority none.org advancedsearch, Crossref, Semantic Scholar rate-limited).

new_statements.quote: The Khalkha Mongolian data are presented below. The generalization is that the first long vowel of the word gets stressed; if there are no long vowels in a word, then the first vowel is stressed. new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive unbounded system: stress the leftmost long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, stress the initial syllable. Agrees with the catalog's 'weight' kind and with Poppe 1970 for words with zero, one or two long vowels (Poppe's 'penultimate long vowel' and Hagberg/Street's 'first long vowel' coincide for two); they diverge only for three or more long vowels (leftmost vs. penultimate), and Hagberg's data contain no such word. Not first-hand: the six forms are taken from Street 1963. The only first-hand statements read in this sweep are the on-disk instrumental papers: Svantesson 1990 (intensity peaks on the first long vowel else the initial vowel, but 'a unified phenomenon of word stress does not exist'), Sang & Martin 2012 (F0 highest on the long vowel, else initial), and Karlsson & Svantesson 2004 (reject lexical stress; prominence is phrasal).

audit.recode_to: Mark as CONTESTED / no-lexical-stress candidate: keep Poppe 1970 + Walker 1997 as the source of the QS 'rightmost nonfinal CVV, else initial' rule but add a caution that the instrumental literature on Halh (Svantesson 1990; Karlsson & Svantesson 2004; Karlsson 2005; Svantesson et al. 2005) finds no unified word stress (phrasal LH accent on the first two morae) and that the one instrumental study that does posit word stress (Sang & Martin 2012, 4 UB speakers) finds leftmost-heavy-else-initial, not rightmost-nonfinal. If the catalog has a 'none/phrasal' or 'contested' kind, move halh1238 there (or set strict=false + caution and drop 'edge: unbounded rightmost' to 'edge: disputed L vs R'); final call after reading Svantesson et al. 2005 ch. on word stress (~p.85-97) and Karlsson 2005.

sources.citation: Sang, Yumei & Philippe Martin. 2012. The role of F0 in Mongolian stress. Speech Prosody 2012 (Shanghai), 575-578. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2012-145
sources.quote: '1. Stress falls on the first syllable for the words with only short vowels. 2. Stress falls on the leftmost syllable containing a long vowel.' In words with several long vowels 'the leftmost long vowel has always the highest Fo value, the longest vowel duration'. Weight-sensitive (CVV) as coded, but leftmost-heavy-else-initial, not Walker's rightmost-nonfinal-heavy.
sources.locator: sec. 3 Discussion and sec. 4 Conclusion, pp.577-578; 4 Ulaanbaatar Halh speakers, 328 di/trisyllabic targets incl. VV-VV-V, VV-VV-VV
sources.note: First-hand acoustic study (4 Ulaanbaatar speakers, 2011): in words with only short vowels the first vowel has the highest F0; in words with a long vowel the long vowel carries the highest F0 (leftmost long vowel in the cited passage). Supports weight-sensitive placement with initial default.

sources.note: General theory dissertation (Mayo is the main case study); Khalkha is one of six 'unbounded' types, treated on ~3 pages with data credited to Street 1963 (Khalkha Structure), not first-hand. Rule stated: stress the first (leftmost) long vowel; if no long vowel, the first vowel. Analysed as Weight-to-Stress applied non-iteratively left-to-right + End Rule Left, no feet. Weight = long vowel only (no mention of closed syllables or diphthongs).

sources.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia Mukhanova & Jan-Olof Svantesson. 2004. Prominence and mora in Mongolian. Speech Prosody 2004 (Nara). doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2004-15
sources.quote: 'Basing ourself on this investigation we reject the existence of lexical stress in Mongolian and find prominence as functioning only at the phrasal level'; focal/word accent is a bitonal LH gesture aligned with the first two morae; long vowels analysed as occurring only in initial syllables (non-initial 'long' vowels = phonemic short, short = epenthetic schwa), which removes the CVV weight basis of the Poppe/Walker rule outside syllable 1.
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction and sec. 2-3; Halh speakers, read speech
sources.note: Rejects lexical (word) stress for Halh; prominence is phrasal (LH gesture anchored to the second mora of the phrase-initial word). Long vowels count two morae; only initial syllables carry phonemic vowels.

sources.citation: Svantesson, Jan-Olof. 1990. Phonetic correlates of stress in Mongolian. Proceedings of ICSLP 90 (Kobe), vol. 1, 617-620. doi:10.21437/ICSLP.1990-178
sources.quote: Abstract: 'The conclusion is that a unified phenomenon of word stress does not exist in Mongolian.' Discussion: 'The four parameters considered here do not cooccur to give prominence to any fixed syllable of a Mongolian word'; intensity data 'the first long vowel of the word has highest intensity, and if there are no long vowels, the initial vowel has highest intensity' (= Poppe 1951 rule: first long vowel else initial, not Poppe 1970 penultimate/rightmost); F0 Low-High 'tied to the first two moras' and judged phrasal.
sources.locator: pp.617-619 (abstract, Discussion, Conclusion); 3 Ulaanbaatar Khalkha speakers, duration/F1-F2/intensity/F0
sources.note: First-hand instrumental study (3 speakers, standard Khalkha). Intensity peaks on the first long vowel, else the initial vowel (matches Street/Hagberg, and Poppe for words with <=2 long vowels); duration and vowel quality favour the initial syllable; F0 patterns differ by speaker. Concludes no unified word stress exists.

sources.citation: Ozcelik, Oner. 2021. L2 acquisition of a complex stress pattern: UG-constrained learning paths in Khalkha Mongolian. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 627797. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.627797
sources.quote: Adopts Walker 1997 (rightmost non-final heavy, else initial) as the working description but reports: Svantesson et al. 2005 'point this out, stating "there are widely differing opinions on the place and nature of word stress in Mongolian" (p. 96), exemplifying at least six different opinions'; argues initial default prominence is intonational, not foot-based (after Gordon 2000; Svantesson et al. 2005). Secondary; no new native-speaker production data on placement.
